# crop regions on a farm map grid

A farm-planning tool reads a character map of a field (one symbol per plot) and reports connected plots of the same crop, their sizes and fence lengths.

This repository holds the Rust implementation (`src/lib.rs`). It is being ported to Python; the port must behave exactly like the specification below, including for malformed input.

## Behaviour

A farm map is a grid: a list of rows, every row a string of the same length **counted in Unicode code points**. Each code
point is a crop symbol (letters, digits, emoji, ...) except the space, which is bare ground. A *region* is a maximal set of
cells with the same crop symbol that are connected through shared edges (up, down, left, right; no diagonals). Rows are 0-based
from the top, columns 0-based from the left. A grid with rows of different length is an error in every function that can report errors (`largest_crop` is never called with one). An empty grid has no cells.

* `region_sizes(grid)`: the number of cells of every region, largest first (equal sizes need no further order).
* `region_at(grid, row, col)`: the size of the region containing that cell; a cell outside the grid or a bare-ground cell is an error.
* `largest_crop(grid)`: the crop symbol (one code point, as a string) of the largest region; among regions of the same largest
  size the one whose first cell comes first in reading order (top to bottom, left to right) wins; no crops gives *absent*.
* `perimeter(grid, row, col)`: the number of cell edges of the region containing that cell that touch the grid border, bare ground, or a
  different crop (same errors as `region_at`).
* `count_regions(grid, crop)`: how many regions have the symbol `crop`; `crop` must be exactly one code point and not a space (else error).

## Functions

* `region_at(grid, row, col)` -> `int`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>, `row`: int, `col`: int)

* `perimeter(grid, row, col)` -> `int`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>, `row`: int, `col`: int)
* `count_regions(grid, crop)` -> `int`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>, `crop`: str)

# crop regions on a farm map grid

A farm-planning tool reads a character map of a field (one symbol per plot) and reports connected plots of the same crop, their sizes and fence lengths.

This repository holds the Python implementation (`grid_regions.py`). It is being ported to JavaScript; the port must behave exactly like the specification below, including for malformed input.

## Behaviour

A farm map is a grid: a list of rows, every row a string of the same length **counted in Unicode code points**. Each code
point is a crop symbol (letters, digits, emoji, ...) except the space, which is bare ground. A *region* is a maximal set of
cells with the same crop symbol that are connected through shared edges (up, down, left, right; no diagonals). Rows are 0-based
from the top, columns 0-based from the left. A grid with rows of different length is an error in every function that can report errors (`largest_crop` is never called with one). An empty grid has no cells.

* `region_sizes(grid)`: the number of cells of every region, largest first (equal sizes need no further order).
* `region_at(grid, row, col)`: the size of the region containing that cell; a cell outside the grid or a bare-ground cell is an error.
* `largest_crop(grid)`: the crop symbol (one code point, as a string) of the largest region; among regions of the same largest
  size the one whose first cell comes first in reading order (top to bottom, left to right) wins; no crops gives *absent*.
* `perimeter(grid, row, col)`: the number of cell edges of the region containing that cell that touch the grid border, bare ground, or a
  different crop (same errors as `region_at`).
* `count_regions(grid, crop)`: how many regions have the symbol `crop`; `crop` must be exactly one code point and not a space (else error).

## Functions

* `region_sizes(grid)` -> `list<int>`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>)
* `region_at(grid, row, col)` -> `int`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>, `row`: int, `col`: int)
* `largest_crop(grid)` -> `opt<str>`. (`grid`: list<str>)
* `perimeter(grid, row, col)` -> `int`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>, `row`: int, `col`: int)
* `count_regions(grid, crop)` -> `int`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>, `crop`: str)

Types: `int` is a signed 64-bit integer and every value in the test vectors is within +-2^53; `str` is Unicode text; `opt<T>` is either a value of `T` or *absent*; `list<T>` is an ordered sequence.

## Python (source)

```python
def region_sizes(grid: list[str]) -> list[int]
def region_at(grid: list[str], row: int, col: int) -> int
def largest_crop(grid: list[str]) -> str | None
def perimeter(grid: list[str], row: int, col: int) -> int
def count_regions(grid: list[str], crop: str) -> int
```

## JavaScript (target)

Create `src/grid_regions.js` (and any extra files you need).

CommonJS module `src/grid_regions.js` whose `module.exports` has one property per function (camelCase names). Numbers are JavaScript numbers; `u32` values are non-negative integers below 2^32; every `i32`/`u32` result must be exactly the value the specification gives. Failure is signalled by throwing an exception. An absent `opt` value is `null`.

```js
regionSizes(grid)   // (grid: string[]) -> number[]
regionAt(grid, row, col)   // (grid: string[], row: number, col: number) -> number
largestCrop(grid)   // (grid: string[]) -> string | null
perimeter(grid, row, col)   // (grid: string[], row: number, col: number) -> number
countRegions(grid, crop)   // (grid: string[], crop: string) -> number
```

## Checking

`test/vectors.test.js` reads the vector file `vectors/examples.json` (a small sample) and calls the JavaScript API; run `node --test test/*.test.js`. The same harness is used with a much larger vector file when the port is graded, so passing the examples only is not enough. The harness files and `vectors/examples.json` must not be edited.

# crop regions on a farm map grid

A farm-planning tool reads a character map of a field (one symbol per plot) and reports connected plots of the same crop, their sizes and fence lengths.

This repository holds the JavaScript implementation (`src/grid_regions.js`). It is being ported to Rust; the port must behave exactly like the specification below, including for malformed input.

## Behaviour

A farm map is a grid: a list of rows, every row a string of the same length **counted in Unicode code points**. Each code
point is a crop symbol (letters, digits, emoji, ...) except the space, which is bare ground. A *region* is a maximal set of
cells with the same crop symbol that are connected through shared edges (up, down, left, right; no diagonals). Rows are 0-based
from the top, columns 0-based from the left. A grid with rows of different length is an error in every function that can report errors (`largest_crop` is never called with one). An empty grid has no cells.

* `region_sizes(grid)`: the number of cells of every region, largest first (equal sizes need no further order).
* `region_at(grid, row, col)`: the size of the region containing that cell; a cell outside the grid or a bare-ground cell is an error.
* `largest_crop(grid)`: the crop symbol (one code point, as a string) of the largest region; among regions of the same largest
  size the one whose first cell comes first in reading order (top to bottom, left to right) wins; no crops gives *absent*.
* `perimeter(grid, row, col)`: the number of cell edges of the region containing that cell that touch the grid border, bare ground, or a
  different crop (same errors as `region_at`).
* `count_regions(grid, crop)`: how many regions have the symbol `crop`; `crop` must be exactly one code point and not a space (else error).

## Functions

* `region_sizes(grid)` -> `list<int>`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>)
* `region_at(grid, row, col)` -> `int`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>, `row`: int, `col`: int)
* `largest_crop(grid)` -> `opt<str>`. (`grid`: list<str>)
* `perimeter(grid, row, col)` -> `int`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>, `row`: int, `col`: int)
* `count_regions(grid, crop)` -> `int`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>, `crop`: str)

Types: `int` is a signed 64-bit integer and every value in the test vectors is within +-2^53; `str` is Unicode text; `opt<T>` is either a value of `T` or *absent*; `list<T>` is an ordered sequence.

## JavaScript (source)

```js
regionSizes(grid)   // (grid: string[]) -> number[]
regionAt(grid, row, col)   // (grid: string[], row: number, col: number) -> number
largestCrop(grid)   // (grid: string[]) -> string | null
perimeter(grid, row, col)   // (grid: string[], row: number, col: number) -> number
countRegions(grid, crop)   // (grid: string[], crop: string) -> number
```

## Rust (target)

The Rust API already exists as stubs (every function fails at run time); replace the bodies.

Crate `grid_regions`: everything is reachable from `src/lib.rs` (extra modules are fine; re-export them). Failure is an `Err(_)` (the error type is yours); never panic on bad input. No dependencies.

```rust
pub fn region_sizes(grid: &[String]) -> Result<Vec<i64>, E>
pub fn region_at(grid: &[String], row: i64, col: i64) -> Result<i64, E>
pub fn largest_crop(grid: &[String]) -> Option<String>
pub fn perimeter(grid: &[String], row: i64, col: i64) -> Result<i64, E>
pub fn count_regions(grid: &[String], crop: &str) -> Result<i64, E>
```

## Checking

`tests/vectors.rs` reads the vector file `vectors/examples.json` (a small sample) and calls the Rust API; run `cargo test --offline`. The same harness is used with a much larger vector file when the port is graded, so passing the examples only is not enough. The harness files and `vectors/examples.json` must not be edited.

# crop regions on a farm map grid

A farm-planning tool reads a character map of a field (one symbol per plot) and reports connected plots of the same crop, their sizes and fence lengths.

This repository holds the Rust implementation (`src/lib.rs`). It is being ported to JavaScript; the port must behave exactly like the specification below, including for malformed input.

## Behaviour

A farm map is a grid: a list of rows, every row a string of the same length **counted in Unicode code points**. Each code
point is a crop symbol (letters, digits, emoji, ...) except the space, which is bare ground. A *region* is a maximal set of
cells with the same crop symbol that are connected through shared edges (up, down, left, right; no diagonals). Rows are 0-based
from the top, columns 0-based from the left. A grid with rows of different length is an error in every function that can report errors (`largest_crop` is never called with one). An empty grid has no cells.

* `region_sizes(grid)`: the number of cells of every region, largest first (equal sizes need no further order).
* `region_at(grid, row, col)`: the size of the region containing that cell; a cell outside the grid or a bare-ground cell is an error.
* `largest_crop(grid)`: the crop symbol (one code point, as a string) of the largest region; among regions of the same largest
  size the one whose first cell comes first in reading order (top to bottom, left to right) wins; no crops gives *absent*.
* `perimeter(grid, row, col)`: the number of cell edges of the region containing that cell that touch the grid border, bare ground, or a
  different crop (same errors as `region_at`).
* `count_regions(grid, crop)`: how many regions have the symbol `crop`; `crop` must be exactly one code point and not a space (else error).

## Functions

* `region_sizes(grid)` -> `list<int>`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>)
* `region_at(grid, row, col)` -> `int`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>, `row`: int, `col`: int)
* `largest_crop(grid)` -> `opt<str>`. (`grid`: list<str>)
* `perimeter(grid, row, col)` -> `int`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>, `row`: int, `col`: int)
* `count_regions(grid, crop)` -> `int`. Fails on invalid input. (`grid`: list<str>, `crop`: str)

Types: `int` is a signed 64-bit integer and every value in the test vectors is within +-2^53; `str` is Unicode text; `opt<T>` is either a value of `T` or *absent*; `list<T>` is an ordered sequence.

## Rust (source)

```rust
pub fn region_sizes(grid: &[String]) -> Result<Vec<i64>, E>
pub fn region_at(grid: &[String], row: i64, col: i64) -> Result<i64, E>
pub fn largest_crop(grid: &[String]) -> Option<String>
pub fn perimeter(grid: &[String], row: i64, col: i64) -> Result<i64, E>
pub fn count_regions(grid: &[String], crop: &str) -> Result<i64, E>
```

## JavaScript (target)

The JavaScript API already exists as stubs (every function fails at run time); replace the bodies.

CommonJS module `src/grid_regions.js` whose `module.exports` has one property per function (camelCase names). Numbers are JavaScript numbers; `u32` values are non-negative integers below 2^32; every `i32`/`u32` result must be exactly the value the specification gives. Failure is signalled by throwing an exception. An absent `opt` value is `null`.

```js
regionSizes(grid)   // (grid: string[]) -> number[]
regionAt(grid, row, col)   // (grid: string[], row: number, col: number) -> number
largestCrop(grid)   // (grid: string[]) -> string | null
perimeter(grid, row, col)   // (grid: string[], row: number, col: number) -> number
countRegions(grid, crop)   // (grid: string[], crop: string) -> number
```

## Checking

`test/vectors.test.js` reads the vector file `vectors/examples.json` (a small sample) and calls the JavaScript API; run `node --test test/*.test.js`. The same harness is used with a much larger vector file when the port is graded, so passing the examples only is not enough. The harness files and `vectors/examples.json` must not be edited.
